extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in online humor websites and the history/operation of Cracked.com
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and standards for producing and curating content on a popular online humor website: editorial voice, formats (listicles, features, video), community workshops, publishing cadence, and social-media optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial voice consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The site needed to 'nail down a voice' to fit within its network and succeed (as noted by Jack O'Brien about Demand Media's role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and maintain a distinctive, consistent editorial voice across articles and series so the site 'fits' the network and audience expectations. Examples: Cracked's blend of pop-culture, bawdy humor, and intellect; voice decisions were driven by editorial leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy editing / editorial gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nothing gets on the homepage without heavy editing" — the site used an editorial team to pick and refine material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rigorous editing and multiple-editor review before promoting content to the homepage. O'Brien and five other editors selected and refined the best material; heavy editing functioned as a quality filter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching process and Writer's Workshop model
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers pitched ideas to the site's on-staff editorial team; the Writer's Workshop (a limited-access virtual writer's room) allowed pitches and peer/editor feedback. More than 90% of top-spot stories came from the Workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a structured pitching system and a workshop to crowdsource ideas while retaining editorial control: greenlight promising pitches, assign and give feedback, and use the workshop as the main funnel for homepage-worthy pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature article length and cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Cracked published two to four articles daily, with feature articles typically 2,000–3,000 words each; feature articles were the most popular content and often pulled ~1 million views in their first week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in longer-form, well-researched feature pieces published at a steady cadence (multiple per day). Prioritize quality long-form features as a driver of traffic and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listicles / numbered-lists as a core comedic format
rubrics_metrics.description: Cracked became known for popular listicles (e.g., 'The 6 Most Insane People To Ever Run For President'); Wired described 'Why Numbered Lists Are Comedy Gold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numbered lists to structure comedic arguments and to create highly clickable, shareable posts. Typical listicle titles use curiosity, surprise, and a clear number to set expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia balance — importance of video content
rubrics_metrics.description: About 30% of Cracked's content was video; the site ran many web series (Agents of Cracked, After Hours, Does Not Compute, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a significant video program alongside written content: develop recurring series, debate formats, sketches, and topical commentary to diversify engagement and audience reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement features: contests and community participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cracked hosted image-manipulation contests (Photoplasty, Pictofacts), daily 'Craptions' caption contests, forums (Pointless Waste of Time) for reader submissions and a Writer's Workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement interactive features and contests to build community, surface user-generated ideas, and feed editorial pipelines; but note that removing these features (as later happened) changes content sourcing and community engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-media-optimized content (image macros, short-form)
rubrics_metrics.description: After acquisition, the site discontinued much reader-generated content in favor of image macro sets created by a few regular contributors because they were more suitable for posting on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design some content specifically for social sharing (short-form, image macros, meme-ready assets) to increase distribution on social platforms, while balancing with long-form flagship pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable roster of regular contributors / columns
rubrics_metrics.description: The front page formerly contained columns by a staff of regular contributors (named writers and columnists) who produced recurring features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain regular staff contributors and recurring columns to provide consistent voice, audience familiarity, and reliable content production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody and satire across formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Cracked produced numerous parodies and satirical series (e.g., Star Wars/Star Trek parodies, 'Honest Commercials', 'Adventures in Jedi School').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ parody/satire as a versatile comedic approach across articles, videos, and sketches; tailor the parody to the format (listicle, sketch, mock-documentary) for best effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/engagement metrics as success criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The article cites page views, unique visitors, video view counts, minutes spent on site, and awards (People's Voice Webby, Streamy Audience Choice) as markers of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track quantitative metrics (page views, unique visitors, watch time) and qualitative recognition (industry awards) to evaluate content performance and inform editorial strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing and ownership decisions impact quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership and staffing changes (purchases, layoffs, firing of key talent) coincided with public criticism and perceived decline in content quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that cost-cutting, layoffs, or ownership changes that remove experienced editorial and creative staff can degrade content quality; prioritize retaining editorial talent to sustain standards.
